transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-21
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Summary: Quick technical deep dive on KV-cache eviction and paging behavior under long-context workloads. Customer seeing frequent evictions when concurrent sessions spike and when they hit long prefix reuse patterns; also curious about interaction with dedicated pools, VPC deployment, and whether quantized kernels change memory pressure.

Topics: KV cache eviction, paging, prefix reuse, long-context sessions, batching impact, quantization memory/latency tradeoffs, VPC deployment diagnostics

Attendees:
- Alex Chen (Redwood AE)
- Priya Singh (Redwood SE)
- Diego Morales (Redwood Ops)
- Maya Patel (Orion Ventures, ML Platform)
- Ethan Ross (Orion Ventures, SRE)
- Lina Korhonen (Orion Ventures, Product)
transcript_full:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll run through what you're seeing with the kv cache evictions, can you give a quick repro and symptom list?
[00:18] Maya Patel: yeah thanks alex. so like, over the last few weeks when our ingest traffic increases and we have many long chat sessions, we start seeing higher token latencies and then a spike in cache misses, and then the runtime logs show repeated 'kv eviction' messages. on dedicated it's a bit better but still happens.
[00:40] Ethan Ross: to add, it's often correlated with a few sessions that have 8k+ prompt history and reuse the same system prompt across many requests, so prefix reuse seems to be a factor. we also saw increased paging to disk on our on-prem nodes.
[01:05] Priya Singh: ok that's helpful. are you using prefix caching with reuse enabled? and what's your configured kv cache size and page size?
[01:18] Maya Patel: default from your quickstart for private: kv_cache_size=8GB, page_size=64MB - we tried raising to 12GB briefly but then the eviction spikes still shifted.
[01:35] Diego Morales: also note our cluster uses mixed GPUs (A10 + A100) and the runtime picks different kernels per device. wondering if heterogeneous kernel memory usage is causing imbalance.
[01:52] Priya Singh: right. two main axes to consider: total memory reserved for kv cache vs model activation allocation, and the heuristics the runtime uses to evict (LRU-ish with prefix affinity). when you have many long contexts that share prefixes, naive LRU can thrash because the prefix region is repeatedly reloaded then evicted.
[02:15] Ethan Ross: that matches what we see. is there a way to pin commonly-reused prefixes to a hot cache region or bump their priority?
[02:25] Priya Singh: we have a prefix_reuse heuristic you can enable - it groups prefix entries and gives them higher eviction score (i.e., less likely to be evicted). it's beta in 2026-06 builds. you should see fewer reloads for shared system prompts.
[02:42] Maya Patel: great - we'll try that. regarding paging, our ops team is seeing lots of page reads from NVMe. is that expected with your paging implementation?
[02:55] Diego Morales: the runtime supports a paging layer for very large KV sizes so that full working set doesn't have to be resident on GPU. paging is async but if your access pattern is random it can create IO bursts. sequential reuse is fine, but many concurrent long sessions with different tails causes thrashing.
[03:20] Alex Chen: can you share your concurrency numbers? batch sizes? and what's your latency SLO?
[03:29] Lina Korhonen: SLOs are 200-400ms P95 for short responses, but for these long sessions we accept higher latencies. concurrency peaks at ~250 req/s across the pool; average batch size is 1-2 tokens, we do some auto-batching at app layer.
[03:50] Priya Singh: small batches mean more KV lookups per GPU step relative to token work, so that increases relative overhead and can surface eviction if cache misses are frequent. increasing auto-batch window slightly can amortize some of that.
[04:10] Ethan Ross: what's the recommended approach for mixed GPU clusters? should we isolate A100s for long-context workloads?
[04:20] Priya Singh: yes, best practice is to route long-context, high-memory sessions to nodes with larger VRAM and consistent kernel profiles. Smart routing can pin requests by policy (latency vs cost) - for Dedicated you can tag pools.
[04:38] Maya Patel: we run private on-prem so tagging is via node labels - doable. but during bursts we still overflow to smaller GPUs which triggers eviction.
[04:50] Diego Morales: one trick is to use a 'cold' fallback model variant that has kv cache disabled but smaller memory footprint - for non-critical tails that's a graceful degradation.
[05:05] Alex Chen: let's talk quantization - you mentioned mixed kernels; if you quantize the model (4-bit) memory drops but activation and perf characteristics change. have you tested eviction behavior under quantized models?
[05:20] Maya Patel: we tried static quantization 4-bit and saw lower memory usage but oddly more frequent evictions in some runs.
[05:30] Priya Singh: that's expected in some cases. quantized kernels may increase activation memory or force different buffer layout, and paging interactions can change. rollout recommendations: test with representative traces, enable detailed kv metrics, and compare hit rates with and without quantization.
[05:55] Ethan Ross: what metrics should we collect to show eviction root cause?
[06:00] Priya Singh: collect: kv_hit_rate, kv_eviction_count, kv_active_entries, page_reads/sec, page_write/sec, GPU_mem_alloc, GPU_mem_free, per-request prefix_hit boolean, kernel_variant used. capture flamegraphs of memory allocation if possible.
[06:28] Maya Patel: ok we'll add those. back to prefix reuse - how aggressive is the grouping? could it starve other entries?
[06:40] Priya Singh: grouping uses a weighted LRU where weight = base_priority + reuse_bonus. reuse_bonus decays over time so it shouldn't permanently starve cold entries. but if your workload is dominated by a small set of prefixes, other entries will naturally be evicted - that's by design.
[06:58] Ethan Ross: we saw scenarios with periodic evictions every ~30s - logs show a churn cadence. is there an internal compaction or periodic GC?
[07:08] Diego Morales: there is a background compaction that reclaims fragmented allocations, it can cause short-lived pressure spikes if triggered simultaneously across nodes. we added jitter in later builds to avoid synchronized compactions.
[07:25] Alex Chen: a reproducible test we often use: run 200 concurrent sessions, each with 6k context, 50% share prefix A and 50% unique tails; then ramp to peak and watch eviction counters. you should see whether prefix reuse avoids thrash.
[07:44] Maya Patel: we can run that. is there a recommended page_size? we used 64MB default
[07:53] Priya Singh: page_size tuning depends on IO and pattern. larger pages reduce metadata overhead but increase wasted reads. for NVMe with many concurrent random reads smaller pages (16-32MB) helped some customers; for SSD that prefers larger pages - start with 32MB and test.
[08:12] Ethan Ross: about observability - are the eviction logs per-shard? we need to correlate across nodes.
[08:19] Priya Singh: yes, logs include shard and stream ids. we also push telemetry to metrics exporter with labels for pool/node/session_id. we'll send a dashboard template.
[08:32] Lina Korhonen: one more question: does the runtime pin KV pages to GPU memory when the same prefix is used frequently?
[08:40] Diego Morales: we do an eager prefetch for high-frequency prefixes in the hot set - but prefetching uses bandwidth; if mispredicted it can increase pressure. enabling prefix_reuse helps make prefetching more accurate.
[08:58] Alex Chen: let's go over a concrete debugging plan - priya?
[09:03] Priya Singh: plan: 1) enable kv debug logging and prefix_reuse; 2) run reproducer that ramps concurrency; 3) collect kv metrics and GPU memory traces; 4) try page_size variations (32MB, 64MB) and optionally reduce page_size if random io is high; 5) test quantized vs non-quantized; 6) if needed, route long-context traffic to A100-only pool or use dedicated capacity.
[09:35] Maya Patel: sounds practical. can you remind us how to enable prefix_reuse?
[09:39] Priya Singh: set runtime flag --kv-prefix-reuse=on and restart the agent; also set kv_cache_prefill=true for warm starts. we'll include CLI snippets.
[09:51] Ethan Ross: when we gather logs, what specific markers will indicate eviction due to paging vs eviction due to memory pressure?
[09:58] Priya Singh: eviction log lines include reason: "pressure" or "page_overflow"; page_overflow indicates IO paging was triggered. also correlated page_reads spikes indicate paging.
[10:12] Maya Patel: earlier you mentioned autoscaling interplay - diego can you expand?
[10:16] Diego Morales: autoscaling sometimes spins up new nodes quickly but redistribution of KV entries isn't immediate, causing temporary duplication of working set and higher combined memory use. also scale-in can evict entries on the nodes being drained which can cause reloading on remaining nodes. configure cooldowns and prefer scale-vertical (if available) for short spikes.
[10:42] Alex Chen: important to include in checklist: cooldowns, pre-warm strategy, and avoid draining nodes with hot prefixes.
[10:52] Lina Korhonen: on security, since we're private/on-prem, any KV cache data written to disk is encrypted at rest?
[10:58] Priya Singh: yes, on Private we integrate with customer KMS and disk-level encryption. page files are encrypted and we redact keys from logs. we'll include the security note.
[11:12] Ethan Ross: ok, let's record the concrete experiments we will run this week.
[11:16] Maya Patel: 1) run 200 concurrent sessions repro with prefix_reuse off, collect metrics; 2) repeat with prefix_reuse on; 3) vary page_size 32/64; 4) quantized vs fp16 runs.
[11:30] Priya Singh: and please include a representative token distribution (how many tokens per request) and the proportion of prefix reuse so we can mirror it in our lab.
[11:42] Alex Chen: anything else?
[11:44] Lina Korhonen: just timing for the next meeting - how soon can we do a joint analysis?
[11:49] Alex Chen: we'll aim for 2026-07-28 for a follow-up with benchmarks visible; priya will prepare a short deck.
[12:00] Closing notes: recap of next steps and owners. thanks everyone.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present ("kv cache" became "k v cache" in one log, some kernel names like cuBLAS spelled as cu-bloss), filler words, and overlapping chatter at times.
